issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette: Seventy-six-year-old Giovanni had always taken pride in his work as a hotel manager. He knew every inch of the building, every staff member by name, and every guest's preference. But it all changed one fateful day when a toxic chemical leak occurred in the hotel's basement, exposing him to noxious fumes. As he struggled to evacuate guests and employees, Giovanni couldn't shake off the feeling that his body had betrayed him. The once-familiar surroundings now seemed treacherous, and his own physical reactions, unpredictable. In the months following the incident, Giovanni found himself increasingly on edge, even in the safety of his own home. He would constantly monitor his thoughts for signs of "going crazy," a fear fueled by his conviction that his body was no longer reliable. His senses were perpetually heightened, and unexpected sounds – the creaking of floorboards or the hum of the refrigerator – made him jump. Giovanni's world had shrunk to a handful of "safe zones" where he felt some semblance of control. The rest of the world seemed like a minefield. Giovanni's memories of that day were fragmented and disjointed, like pieces of a puzzle that refused to fit together. He would recall the acrid smell of chemicals, only to have it vanish without warning. Other times, he'd feel an overwhelming sense of dread without any clear image or memory attached. These disjointed recollections kept him up at night, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. As Giovanni struggled to make sense of these fragmented memories, he began to avoid the hotel altogether. The mere thought of stepping foot in that building sent his anxiety soaring. He'd try to distract himself with loud music or TV, but the sounds only seemed to amplify his unease. Giovanni felt trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance, unable to escape the grip of his own memories. His negative appraisals of himself and his body – "My body keeps reacting as if I'm still in danger even when I'm safe" – reinforced this sense of helplessness. Giovanni couldn't shake off the feeling that he was at the mercy of his own reactions, powerless to stop bad things from happening to him. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Giovanni's world continued to shrink. His relationships suffered, and even simple tasks seemed insurmountable. It wasn't until a particularly harrowing episode – where he found himself crippled by anxiety in the middle of his own living room – that Giovanni realized he needed help. He couldn't continue living like this, trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and avoidance. What finally brought Giovanni to seek therapy was the realization that he was losing himself in this labyrinth of memories and fears. He longed for a sense of control over his body and mind, to be able to trust himself again. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, Giovanni whispered, "I just want to feel safe in my own skin."
